subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Population and Migration
subtitle: Reading pack for KS3 population and migration case studies and data skills.
description: Reading passages for KS3 Geography on population distribution, natural change, population pyramids, migration causes and migration impacts. Each passage includes retrieval, inference and explanation questions.

data.sourcePassage: Population distribution means the pattern of where people live. Population density measures how crowded a place is by dividing the total population by the area. A place with 500 people per km2 is more densely populated than a place with 20 people per km2. The UK population is unevenly distributed. London, Birmingham and Manchester have high densities because they have jobs, services and transport links. Upland areas such as the Scottish Highlands and central Wales are more sparsely populated because relief can be steep, transport links are weaker and there are fewer large settlements.

questions.question: What does population distribution mean?
questions.modelAnswer: It means the pattern of where people live.

questions.question: Which formula is used for population density?
questions.modelAnswer: Population density = population divided by area.

questions.question: Why are major UK cities often densely populated?
questions.modelAnswer: They often have more jobs, services and transport links, which attract people and support large populations.

questions.question: Why can upland areas be sparsely populated?
questions.modelAnswer: Upland areas can have steep relief, weaker transport links and fewer large settlements or jobs.

questions.question: Explain why a larger total population does not always mean higher population density.
questions.modelAnswer: Density depends on population and area. A large population spread over a very large area can have a lower density than a smaller population in a small area.

data.sourcePassage: Population changes when people are born, die, move into an area or move out of an area. Natural change is calculated by subtracting the death rate from the birth rate. If the birth rate is higher than the death rate, the population has natural increase. If the death rate is higher, it has natural decrease. The demographic transition model shows how birth and death rates may change as a country develops. In Stage 2, death rates often fall because healthcare, food and sanitation improve. In Stage 3, birth rates often fall as education, living standards and job opportunities improve.

questions.question: What are the four main causes of population change named in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Births, deaths, immigration and emigration.

questions.question: What happens when birth rate is higher than death rate?
questions.modelAnswer: The population has natural increase.

questions.question: Calculate natural change if birth rate is 22 and death rate is 7.
questions.modelAnswer: 22 - 7 = 15 per 1,000 people per year.

questions.question: Why might death rates fall in Stage 2 of the DTM?
questions.modelAnswer: Healthcare, food supply and sanitation may improve, so fewer people die from disease or poor living conditions.

questions.question: Why is the DTM useful but not perfect?
questions.modelAnswer: It helps geographers understand broad patterns, but it is a simplified model and does not exactly fit every country.

data.sourcePassage: A population pyramid shows the age and sex structure of a population. Males are usually shown on the left, females on the right, young age groups at the bottom and older groups at the top. A wide base suggests many children and a youthful population. A narrow base with larger older age groups suggests an ageing population. Japan is often used as an ageing population example because it has high life expectancy and low birth rates. Nigeria is often used as a youthful population example because it has a high proportion of children and young adults. Japan may need more healthcare and pension support, whereas Nigeria may need more schools, housing and future jobs.

questions.question: What does a population pyramid show?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows the age and sex structure of a population.

questions.question: What does a wide base on a population pyramid usually suggest?
questions.modelAnswer: It suggests many children and usually a high birth rate.
options: Low life expectancy in every case

questions.question: Why is Japan described as an ageing population example?
questions.modelAnswer: Japan has high life expectancy, low birth rates and a high proportion of older people.

questions.question: Compare one planning challenge for Japan and Nigeria.
questions.modelAnswer: Japan may need more healthcare, elderly care and pension support, while Nigeria may need more schools, housing and future jobs for young people.

questions.question: Why should geographers avoid saying older people are a problem?
questions.modelAnswer: The challenge is the age structure and planning need, not older people themselves. Older people can also contribute skills, work, volunteering and family support.

data.sourcePassage: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. It can be internal, such as moving from Manchester to Leeds, or international, such as moving from Spain to the UK. It can be voluntary, such as moving for university, or forced, such as leaving a country because of war, persecution or violence. A refugee is forced to leave their country because they face serious danger. An asylum seeker has asked another country for protection and is waiting for a decision. Migration often has several causes. Someone may be pushed by low wages or conflict and pulled by jobs, safety, education or family links.

questions.question: What is migration?
questions.modelAnswer: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another.

questions.question: Moving from Manchester to Leeds is which type of migration?
questions.modelAnswer: It is internal migration because it happens within one country.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a refugee and an asylum seeker.
questions.modelAnswer: A refugee has been forced to leave their country because of serious danger. An asylum seeker has asked another country for protection and is waiting for a decision.

questions.question: Why is it weak to say people migrate for only one reason?
questions.modelAnswer: Many migrations involve several linked reasons, such as push factors in the origin area and pull factors in the destination.

questions.question: Give one respectful reason why careful language matters when discussing refugees.
questions.modelAnswer: Refugees are people facing serious danger, not just statistics, so careful language avoids stereotypes and recognises human experiences.

data.section: Migration Impacts on Origin and Destination Areas
data.sourceTitle: Migration Impacts on Origin and Destination Areas
data.targetTitle: Migration Impacts on Origin and Destination Areas
data.sourcePassage: Migration affects the places people leave, the places they move to, migrants themselves and their families. Origin areas may receive remittances, which can help families pay for food, education or housing. They may also lose young adults or skilled workers, creating labour shortages or brain drain. Destination areas may benefit when migrants fill job vacancies, pay taxes and add cultural diversity. However, if population grows faster than planning, housing, transport, schools and healthcare can come under pressure. A balanced answer explains both benefits and challenges and uses examples such as rural-urban migration in China or international migration linked to the UK.

questions.question: What are remittances?
questions.modelAnswer: Remittances are money migrants send back to family or communities in origin areas.

questions.question: Which impact mainly affects an origin area?
questions.modelAnswer: Brain drain mainly affects an origin area because skilled workers leave.

questions.question: Give one benefit migration can bring to a destination area.
questions.modelAnswer: Migrants may fill job vacancies, pay taxes, spend money locally or add cultural diversity.

questions.question: Why can rapid migration create pressure on destination services?
questions.modelAnswer: If population grows faster than planning, housing, transport, schools and healthcare may not have enough capacity.

questions.question: What makes an answer about migration impacts balanced?
questions.modelAnswer: It considers both positives and negatives, and looks at origin areas, destination areas, migrants and families using evidence or examples.
